{"summary":"The design automates the mechanical steps of refund processing (verifying orders, matching warehouse returns, issuing Stripe refunds, notifying customers) while preserving a mandatory human finance-approval checkpoint, because the input states both a 'no human involvement' target and a hard auditor rule requiring finance sign-off, and these two stated constraints cannot both hold. The design keeps the auditor control since it is described as a hard requirement, and treats full automation as unattainable at the approval step; it also cannot honour a 60-second refund SLA because the input separately states a fixed once-daily 4pm finance batch and a once-daily 3PL CSV feed, both of which gate the refund before Stripe issuance.","data_flow_description":"A refund request enters via the Zendesk support inbox and is captured by an intake component, which extracts the order reference and opens a refund case. That case is passed to a Shopify verification step that confirms the order exists and pulls order details. The case then waits for the corresponding warehouse return record, which arrives only once a day as a CSV from the 3PL, so cases accumulate until that file lands and a match is found. Matched, verified cases are placed in a queue for the daily 4pm finance review, where a person approves or rejects. Approved cases are sent to Stripe to issue the refund, and the result triggers a customer notification email. Rejected cases exit the flow without a Stripe call. Because the CSV feed and the finance batch are both daily and fixed, no case can complete in under roughly a day, which is irreconcilable with a 60-second issuance target stated elsewhere.","components":[{"name":"Zendesk Intake Listener","responsibility":"Detect and capture a new refund request from the support inbox and open a tracked refund case","inputs":"Incoming Zendesk ticket content","outputs":"A new refund case record with ticket/order reference","failure_handling":"If ticket data cannot be parsed for an order reference, the case is not created and the request remains an unactioned ticket for manual handling","external_system":"Zendesk","integration_direction":"inbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[8]},{"name":"Shopify Order Verification","responsibility":"Confirm the referenced order exists in Shopify and retrieve its order details","inputs":"Order reference from the refund case","outputs":"Verified order data (or a not-found result) attached to the case","failure_handling":"If the order cannot be found or the Shopify lookup fails, the case is held and not passed forward for warehouse matching","external_system":"Shopify","integration_direction":"inbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[7,5]},{"name":"Warehouse Return Confirmation Matcher","responsibility":"Match a refund case against the 3PL's daily return-confirmation CSV to confirm the returned item was received","inputs":"Verified refund case; daily 3PL CSV file","outputs":"A match/no-match result attached to the case","failure_handling":"If no match is found in the day's file, the case is held over to be re-checked against the next day's CSV rather than proceeding","external_system":"3PL warehouse system","integration_direction":"inbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[6,7]},{"name":"Finance Approval Queue","responsibility":"Hold verified, return-matched refund cases for mandatory human finance review during the fixed daily batch window","inputs":"Verified and warehouse-matched refund cases","outputs":"Approved or rejected decision per case","failure_handling":"If the daily 4pm review does not occur or is incomplete, cases remain queued and no refund is issued until a decision is recorded","external_system":null,"integration_direction":null,"grounded_in_context_indices":[1,3]},{"name":"Stripe Refund Issuance","responsibility":"Execute the refund payment for cases that have received finance approval","inputs":"Approved refund case with order and amount data","outputs":"Refund transaction result (success/failure) from Stripe","failure_handling":"If the Stripe call fails, the case is flagged as unresolved and does not proceed to customer notification; it is not retried automatically without a stated retry rule","external_system":"Stripe","integration_direction":"outbound","grounded_in_context_indices":[5,7]},{"name":"Customer Notification Emailer","responsibility":"Notify the customer once a refund decision (issued or not) has been finalised","inputs":"Refund transaction result","outputs":"Outbound email to the customer","failure_handling":"If the email fails to send, the refund itself is unaffected but the customer is not informed, leaving a gap the process does not otherwise cover","external_system":null,"integration_direction":null,"grounded_in_context_indices":[7]}],"unknown_disposition":[{"context_index":9,"disposition":"excluded","statement":"No differentiated approval path or threshold is built for high-value (e.g. up to £2,000) refunds; all cases pass through the single daily finance approval queue until the input specifies whether bulk-order refunds need a distinct or additional control."},{"context_index":10,"disposition":"deferred","statement":"The design does not assume a build/maintenance model; whether this requires a no-code platform operable by non-developers or can rely on custom integration work is left open pending confirmation of in-house capability."},{"context_index":11,"disposition":"excluded","statement":"No cost-bound choices (e.g. platform tier, integration complexity ceiling) are made in this architecture; budget constraints are left for a later stage once a figure is known."}],"trade_offs":[],"rejected_approaches":[]}

{"factors":[{"factor":"workflow","score":3,"justification":"Sequential path from Zendesk intake through Shopify verification, warehouse match, finance approval, Stripe issuance and notification, with holds/branches at each verification gate (no-match hold, rejection exit, failed-call flag) but no loops or parallel paths — a moderate number of steps with several conditional branch points."},{"factor":"integration","score":3,"justification":"Four external systems (Zendesk, Shopify, 3PL CSV, Stripe) plus email notification, each with conventional if heterogeneous interfaces (ticketing API, e-commerce API, daily batch file, payment API); none are described as poorly documented, but the mix of real-time APIs and a daily batch file adds heterogeneity beyond a single-system case."},{"factor":"data_logic","score":2,"justification":"Data largely passes through with matching/lookup logic (order reference matching, CSV return matching, approval status) rather than substantial reshaping; rules are recognisable but not extensive — matching a case to a CSV row and gating on approval status, no reconciliation across many sources or dense rule interactions."},{"factor":"failure_risk","score":4,"justification":"The design has several distinct failure modes (unparseable ticket, order not found, no CSV match, missed finance batch, failed Stripe call, failed email) each requiring deliberate handling, and it moves real money via Stripe with no stated retry rule for failed refund calls, plus an unresolved conflict between a 60-second SLA and daily batch/CSV gating that the design itself flags as irreconcilable — a demanding correctness situation."},{"factor":"operational","score":3,"justification":"The daily finance approval batch requires routine recurring human attention (index 1, 3), and held/unmatched cases (no CSV match, failed Stripe calls, undelivered emails) need periodic manual follow-up, though volume is modest (200/week) and the process does not need continuous monitoring."}]}

The whole design as specified now exists.","estimate":null}],"sequencing_rationale":"The order follows the data flow the architecture itself describes: each component consumes the output of the one before it, so building out of order would leave a stage with nothing to act on. Intake must exist before there is a case to verify; Shopify verification must exist before a case can be checked against the 3PL return file, since the matcher operates on verified cases; the warehouse match must exist before finance review, because only matched cases are described as entering the approval queue; finance approval must exist before Stripe issuance, since Stripe issuance is defined to act only on approved cases (the hard auditor control from context 1 is therefore proven before any payment logic is built, rather than being bolted on afterward); and notification is last because it consumes the Stripe transaction result. The two irreconcilable stated constraints — the 60-second SLA (context 2) and the fixed daily batch plus daily CSV (contexts 3 and 6) — are not treated as separate 'hardening' work: the batch and CSV cadences are built directly into Phases 3 and 4, so the SLA's unreachability is evident as soon as those phases exist rather than discovered later.
